messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai, a 63-year-old Samoan-American publisher, still remembers the day his office building caught fire due to an electrical malfunction. The sound of shattering glass and the smell of smoke are forever etched in his mind. As he recounts the event, his eyes widen, and his voice trembles. He recalls seeing colleagues rushing for the exits, their faces filled with panic. These vivid images (Vivid Memory) continue to haunt him, forcing their way into his mind uninvited (Uncontrolled Access). When they resurface, Kai is often overcome with a sense of dread, as if he's reliving that fateful day. The traumatic event has led to an array of maladaptive strategies that have become ingrained in Kai's daily life. He now always sits with his back against the wall (Sit With Back to Wall), allowing him to survey his surroundings for potential threats. This constant vigilance is a direct response to the memories of that day, when he felt powerless and exposed. Even in his own home, Kai feels the need to be on guard (Alert at Home), as if danger could strike at any moment. He's become increasingly jumpy (Startle Response) and startles easily at ordinary sounds (Startle to Sounds). These exaggerated responses are, in part, a result of his memories, which have conditioned him to associate certain stimuli with life-threatening situations. Kai's maladaptive strategies also influence the way he interacts with others. He has begun avoiding friends (Avoid Friends), fearing that social gatherings will trigger memories of the event or force him to confront emotions he'd rather suppress. When he does venture out, Kai finds himself constantly scanning his environment for signs of threat (Checking Surroundings). This hypervigilance not only reinforces his sense of danger but also perpetuates the cycle of maladaptive behaviors. As Kai navigates his daily life, certain triggers can transport him back to that traumatic event. The smell of alcohol (Olfactory: Alcohol), for instance, might evoke memories of the fire's aftermath, when paramedics and firefighters were present, some of whom were drinking coffee laced with whiskey to calm their nerves. Even waking up from a nightmare (Dream Residue) can leave Kai feeling shaken and on edge. Talking about the event itself (Event Recall) is another potent trigger, as it forces him to relive those harrowing moments. Kai's maladaptive strategies have also become self-reinforcing, perpetuating the cycle of threat and anxiety. By constantly scanning his surroundings, he creates an environment in which he feels perpetually on edge (Threat). This sense of danger, in turn, fuels his memories (Memory), making them feel even more vivid and intrusive. As Kai becomes increasingly entrenched in this cycle, it's clear that he needs help to break free from the grip of his traumatic past. Kai's decision to seek therapy was motivated by a recent incident in which he became convinced that an ordinary noise was a sign of danger (Startle to Sounds). His wife, concerned about his escalating anxiety, urged him to get professional help. As Kai begins this new chapter, he's hoping to learn how to manage his memories and reduce his sense of threat. He's most afraid of losing control, but with the right guidance, he's willing to confront his fears and work towards a more peaceful life.
